content.overview: BNS s. 52 — Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done. BNS restatement of IPC 112. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 112. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 52 is the rule on “Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done”. The section provides that if the act for which the abettor is liable under section 51 is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitute a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 52 exists so that “Abettor when liable to cumulative punishment for act abetted and for act done” has a closed legal test in Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: The inchoate trio. Abetment now covers extra-territorial aid; conspiracy and attempt sit next to it.

The provision in detail
52. If the act for which the abettor is liable under section 51 is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitute a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences

Essential ingredients
1. If the act for which the abettor is liable under section 51 is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitute a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A instigates B to resist by force a distress made by a public servant. B, in consequence, resists that distress. In offering the resistance, B voluntarily causes grievous hurt to the officer executing the distress. As B has committed both the offence of resisting the distress, and the offence of voluntarily causing grievous hurt, B is liable to punishment for both these offences; and, if A knew that B was likely voluntarily to cause grievous hurt in resisting the distress, A will also be liable to punishment for each of the offences

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 52 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

learningObjectives: Understand when an abettor faces cumulative (separate) punishment under BNS s. 52.
Analyze the requirement that both the abetted act and the different act were committed and constitute distinct offences.
Examine the application of s. 52 in conjunction with s. 51.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 52 provides that if the act for which the abettor is liable under the last preceding section is committed in addition to the act abetted, and constitutes a distinct offence, the abettor is liable to punishment for each of the offences.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Where the perpetrator successfully commits the original abetted crime AND additionally commits a distinct, probable consequence offence, the abettor is cumulatively punishable for both distinct offences.
statutoryFramework: Chapter IV — Of Abetment, Criminal Conspiracy and Attempt, BNS s. 52 (corresponding to IPC s. 112).
Prerequisite 1: Liability established under s. 51 for the different act.
Prerequisite 2: The different act is committed 'in addition to' the act abetted.
Prerequisite 3: The two acts constitute 'distinct offences'.
Penalty: Abettor is liable to punishment 'for each of the offences' (cumulative sentencing).
essentialIngredients: The abettor is liable under s. 51 for a different act done.
The original act abetted was also actually committed.
The two acts constitute separate, distinct offences under the law.
The abettor is sentenced cumulatively for both offences.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 52 is the sentencing companion to Section 51. In many cases of escalation, the perpetrator does not merely substitute one act for another; he commits BOTH. For example, A instigates B to resist a court bailiff seizing cattle. B resists the bailiff (act abetted), and in the struggle, B also severely fractures the bailiff's arm (grievous hurt — probable consequence). Here, two distinct offences occurred: resisting a public servant AND grievous hurt. Under s. 52, A is not merely punished for one; he is liable to cumulative punishment for both distinct crimes.
examples: Teaching example (Resisting arrest and grievous hurt): A instigates B to resist a lawful arrest by a police officer. B resists the arrest, and in doing so, inflicts grievous hurt on the officer with a baton. Both offences are distinct and committed. Under s. 52, A is liable to cumulative punishment for abetting resistance to arrest AND for abetting grievous hurt.

Teaching example (Robbery and murder): A instigates B to commit robbery. B commits robbery and, in the course of it, murders the cashier (probable consequence). A is liable to cumulative punishment for robbery and murder under s. 52.
distinctions: Section 51 vs Section 52: Section 51 determines substantive liability for the different act; Section 52 authorizes cumulative sentencing when both the abetted act and different act are committed.
Single composite act vs Distinct offences: If the different act completely replaces the abetted act, s. 52 does not apply; s. 52 requires both acts to have taken place.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an abettor who planned a house burglary is cumulatively liable when the burglar both stole the jewelry and assaulted the night watchman.
Rule: Under BNS s. 52, if the act abetted and the distinct probable consequence act are both committed, cumulative punishment is imposed for each.
Application: The burglary was committed, and the assault was committed in addition as a probable consequence. They are distinct offences.
Conclusion: The abettor is subject to cumulative punishment for both offences under s. 52.
